lessons.title: Introduction to SQL Subqueries
lessons.description: Understand nested queries, scalar subqueries and subqueries in WHERE clauses.
lessons.content:
A subquery is a SELECT statement nested inside another SQL statement. The inner query produces a value or result set that the outer query uses. Subqueries commonly appear in WHERE, FROM and SELECT clauses.

Example tables: employees(employee_id, name, salary, department_id) and departments(department_id, department_name).

To find employees earning above the company average:

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
);

The inner SELECT calculates the average salary. The outer SELECT returns employees whose salaries exceed that value.

A scalar subquery returns one column and at most one row. It can be compared using operators such as =, > and <. If it returns multiple rows, a scalar comparison normally produces an error.

Subqueries improve readability when a query depends on a calculated value. However, not every subquery is faster than a JOIN. Database optimizers may transform subqueries internally.

Interview tip: Identify what the inner query returns before analyzing the outer query.

lessons.title: IN, NOT IN, ANY and ALL Subqueries
lessons.description: Use subqueries returning multiple values to filter records.
lessons.content:
A subquery can return multiple rows. The IN operator checks whether a value belongs to the returned set.

Find employees working in departments located in Bengaluru:

SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (
  SELECT department_id
  FROM departments
  WHERE location = 'Bengaluru'
);

NOT IN selects values absent from a set, but NULL values require special care. If the subquery returns NULL, NOT IN may return no matching rows because SQL uses three-valued logic. NOT EXISTS is often safer for anti-matching queries.

ANY compares a value with at least one value returned by a subquery. ALL requires the comparison to hold for every returned value.

Example:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > ALL (
  SELECT salary
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id = 10
);

This returns employees earning more than every non-NULL salary in department 10, assuming the subquery contains salaries. If the subquery is empty, the ALL condition is true; NULL comparisons may yield UNKNOWN.

Choose IN for membership, EXISTS for checking matching rows, and ALL or ANY when the comparison logic specifically requires them.

lessons.title: Correlated Subqueries and EXISTS
lessons.description: Learn how inner queries reference the current row of an outer query.
lessons.content:
A correlated subquery references a column from its surrounding query. Conceptually, the condition is evaluated for each candidate outer row, although the database optimizer may execute it differently.

Find employees whose salaries exceed their own department's average:

SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees AS e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
  FROM employees AS e2
  WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id
);

The reference e.department_id connects the inner query to the current employee.

EXISTS returns TRUE when its subquery produces at least one row. The selected expressions inside EXISTS do not determine the result; SELECT 1 is conventional.

Find departments containing at least one employee:

SELECT d.department_name
FROM departments AS d
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM employees AS e
  WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id
);

Find departments with no employees:

SELECT d.department_name
FROM departments AS d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM employees AS e
  WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id
);

EXISTS is useful for checking relationships without duplicating outer rows. Always use aliases to distinguish inner and outer references.

lessons.title: GROUP BY, HAVING and Nested Aggregations
lessons.description: Filter grouped results and combine aggregation with subqueries.
lessons.content:
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has calculated aggregates.

Find departments with at least three employees:

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column_name) counts only non-NULL values in that column.

To find departments whose average salary exceeds the overall company average:

SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS average_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
);

The subquery calculates the company average, while the outer query groups employees by department.

A common logical processing order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT and ORDER BY. This helps explain why aggregate functions generally belong in HAVING rather than WHERE.

Avoid selecting nonaggregated columns that are neither grouped nor functionally dependent on grouping columns. Different database engines enforce grouping rules differently.

Interview tip: Use WHERE for row-level filtering and HAVING for aggregate-based filtering.

lessons.title: Derived Tables, CTEs and Advanced Query Patterns
lessons.description: Organize complex SQL using FROM subqueries and common table expressions.
lessons.content:
A derived table is a subquery inside the FROM clause. It behaves like a temporary result set within the statement and normally requires an alias.

Example:

SELECT department_id, average_salary
FROM (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS average_salary
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department_id
) AS department_stats
WHERE average_salary > 50000;

A common table expression (CTE) gives a named result set using WITH:

WITH department_stats AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS average_salary
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT department_id, average_salary
FROM department_stats
WHERE average_salary > 50000;

CTEs can make long queries easier to understand and maintain. A CTE is not necessarily stored permanently or executed only once; behavior depends on the database optimizer.

Advanced queries may combine JOIN, EXISTS, GROUP BY, HAVING and CTEs. Break complex requirements into smaller logical steps: identify source tables, define relationships, apply row filters, aggregate if needed, and finally filter or sort results.

Performance considerations include indexes on join and filter columns, avoiding unnecessary SELECT *, and examining query plans with EXPLAIN. Compare alternative queries using actual execution plans rather than assuming one syntax is always faster.

Practice writing the same problem using a subquery, a JOIN and a CTE, then explain the readability and performance trade-offs.

quizzes.question: What is a subquery in SQL?
options: A query nested inside another SQL statement
quizzes.explanation: A subquery is a SELECT statement used inside another SQL statement.

quizzes.question: Which operator checks whether a value belongs to a set returned by a subquery?
quizzes.explanation: IN tests membership in a list or subquery result.

quizzes.question: Which clause filters groups based on aggregate values?
What makes a subquery correlated?
options: It references a column from the outer query
quizzes.explanation: A correlated subquery depends on values from its surrounding query.

quizzes.question: What does EXISTS test?
options: Whether a subquery returns at least one row
Whether a table has a primary key
Whether a query contains GROUP BY
quizzes.explanation: EXISTS evaluates to TRUE when the subquery produces at least one row.

quizzes.question: Which expression finds employees earning above the company average?
quizzes.explanation: A scalar subquery calculates the average salary for comparison.

quizzes.question: What is a common problem with NOT IN when the subquery returns NULL?
options: It may return no rows because comparisons become UNKNOWN
It automatically converts to INNER JOIN
quizzes.explanation: NULL values in a NOT IN result can make the predicate UNKNOWN for candidate rows.

quizzes.question: Which SQL keyword begins a common table expression?
quizzes.explanation: WITH introduces one or more common table expressions.

quizzes.question: Where is a derived table written?
quizzes.explanation: A derived table is a subquery used as a table expression in FROM.

quizzes.question: What does > ALL (subquery) mean for a nonempty result containing no NULLs?
options: Greater than at least one returned value
Equal to the maximum returned value
quizzes.explanation: ALL requires the comparison to be true for every value in the subquery result.

exercises.title: Employees Above Average Salary
exercises.description: Use a scalar subquery to compare employee salaries against the company average.
exercises.instructions: Table: employees(employee_id, employee_name, salary, department_id). Write a query returning employee_name and salary for employees whose salary is greater than the average salary of all employees. Use a subquery with AVG(salary).

exercises.title: Employees in Bengaluru Departments
exercises.description: Use IN with a subquery to filter employees by department location.
exercises.instructions: Tables: employees(employee_id, employee_name, department_id) and departments(department_id, department_name, location). Return employee_name for employees whose department is located in Bengaluru. Use WHERE department_id IN (SELECT ...).

exercises.title: Employees Above Their Department Average
exercises.description: Solve a department-based salary comparison using a correlated subquery.
exercises.instructions: Table: employees(employee_id, employee_name, salary, department_id). Return employee_name, department_id and salary for employees earning more than the average salary of their own department. Use table aliases and a correlated AVG subquery.

exercises.title: Departments Without Employees
exercises.description: Identify departments with no matching employees using NOT EXISTS.
exercises.instructions: Tables: departments(department_id, department_name) and employees(employee_id, employee_name, department_id). Return department_id and department_name for departments containing no employees. Use NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery.

exercises.title: High-Paying Departments Using HAVING and CTE
exercises.description: Combine grouping, aggregate filtering and common table expressions.
exercises.instructions: Table: employees(employee_id, employee_name, salary, department_id). Write one query using GROUP BY and HAVING to return departments whose average salary exceeds the overall company average. Then write an equivalent query using WITH to calculate department averages. Return department_id and average_salary.
